cards.title: Scion is back and is going to sell a kei truck in America

depth.text: Toyota is bringing **Scion back** with a **kei truck** meant for slow, local work

The **KEI-01** is a rebadged Toyota Pixis, itself a rebadged Daihatsu Hijet Jumbo Cab; it has a 660cc engine, tops out below 25 mph, and is only legal on roads posted below 35 mph. Toyota says it will start with a **low-volume fleet pilot** in late 2027.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the 25 mph cap makes it impractical for commuting and errands; others say the truck is useful for farms, golf courses, resorts, or local hauling.

comments.text: I use a kei truck for farming. They are incredibly pragmatic little vehicles. They are very capable driving around on dirt/gravel agricultural roads with 4WD, and they are inexpensive and robust enough that you can really beat them up and use them as a tool without worry. Repairs and replacement parts are ubiquitous and inexpensive. Having the sides of bed fold down is also really useful. They…

25 mph works for golf courses, resort, or island use. In rural areas on the mainland, roads connecting towns often have 45 or 55 mph speed limits so unless you plan on staying on the farm I don't think these are practical for trips to go shopping, dumping, hauling, etc. As for the imports, I saw one of these 90s-era right-hand drive kei trucks at a parking lot a few months ago and talked with the…

With a built in 25mph limiter, that eliminates "city" driving too unfortunately. Most roads around me are 35 mph. There's sizeable demand for people who want to be able to do runs to the bigbox stores for garden and DIY renovation supplies and store it the rest of the time.

This would have been an instant buy for me if it weren't for the 25mph limit. That being said, I'm extremely excited by this, because it proves there is demand for Kei trucks in the US. I've done a lot of research into the import process for bringing a truck over from Japan, and I'll likely end up going that route in a year or so unless newer trucks with higher speeds get announced

660cc engine at ~40 horsepower is about the same as a mid-70s VW Beetle - not in cc size, but HP potential. This little truck could do a lot more than 25 mph if it were allowed to do so. Not saying that would be safe, and I'd not want to ever put one on a busy freeway, but for getting around most urban cities in the US it's fine as-is but would be even better if the limit was ~40 mph.

cards.title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers

cards.title: AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast

depth.text: AMD is giving its next CPUs **two core designs**: one tuned for **high clocks**, one for memory delays

Zen 6c gets **larger out-of-order structures** than Zen 6: its reorder buffer grows from 576 to 640 entries, and its load queue from 280 to 330. Its 32-core CCD has **128 MB of L3 cache**, versus 48 MB in Zen 6's 12-core CCD. At a matched 4.1 GHz, Zen 6c is about **6.7% ahead per clock** in integer performance and 4% in floating point.
data: L3 cache (12-core Zen 6 CCD → 32-core Zen 6c CCD)

comments.text: The worst thing about consumer (AM5) Zen4 and Zen5 is the I/O die chiplet and memory controller on it. I've heard they're finally going to ship a new I/O chiplet in Zen6 on a much smaller node. Their existing AM5 Zen4/5 memory controller when using both memory channels is terrible. Extremely hard or impossible to get above 3600 MT/s. Of all the things I'm looking forward to on Zen6, an improved…

The instruction level parallelism in the 2-ahead branch prediction is super cool stuff, I know zen5 had this feature but it's kind of crazy that memory is so slow relative to the cores that this complexity is beneficial and worthwhile.

> AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two. What looks like a lot of small balanced improvements to the core itself. Four vector loads per cycle at 256b of less, I wonder if the gather performance is finally acceptable? Another balance example, they actually reduced the number of integer multipliers down to two. I wonder if that was to make diespace for the vnni pipes? The real star looks like the c cores though. 32 C cores per chiplet…

cards.title: Fossil CO2 emissions decrease in 2026

depth.text: fossil emissions are expected to **dip**, while land-use changes push **total CO2 emissions higher**

The 2026 Global Carbon Budget projects fossil-fuel emissions at 38.2 billion tonnes, down **0.4%**, but total CO2 emissions will rise to **43.3 billion tonnes** from 42.8 billion last year as land-use emissions increase. Solar, wind and electric vehicles are meeting two thirds of rising energy demand, but clean-energy growth is not yet fast enough for a durable decline. The drop is partly driven by the **Iran conflict**.

depth.text: a post says nobody understands the code a year after a **100% AI mandate**

One commenter says they inherited an **AI-written project** that was an **architectural mess** with a breaking bug; another says the senior developers had left, leaving a tiny crew. Others say codebases were hard to understand even before AI.

cards.camps: Some commenters call the post fake or anti-AI engagement bait; others say the experience matches what they’ve seen at work.

comments.text: If you put this into pangram it is 100% AI generated. People on reddit/ youtube are engagement farming anti ai content... with ai text and scripts etc. The actual content is somewhat relatable but don't fall for the bait.

I have a friend who works at a large F100 and in his 12 years as a dev, he has never dreaded his job as he does now. He's working 10 hrs. a day, just entering things into Claude, waiting, reviewing, and learning absolutely nothing. At this point anyone who was truly passionate about programming, is just less and less motivated to become a better engineer.

I sympathize with this, and the company I work for is far less than a year into our mandate. I've recently gained ownership of a project built by a colleague who just left, and... it's horrifying. 100% vibe-coded -- said colleague admitted as much, that he hadn't written code himself for months, and that I should just "ask Claude" if I want to do anything with the project. It's an architectural…

If models are getting exponentially cheaper and more powerful, going all in a year ago is kind of insane. There's ostensibly this reverse token value inflation where whatever you spend on AI today, you'll get much more for the same dollar tomorrow (assuming models get cheaper and better). There's really a weird sort of late mover's advantage to just holding off and saving your money unless you…

AI is an accelerator. In this case it accelerated piling up the tech debt. There's no reason they couldn't have paused the relentless production of features to do a few runs of cleaning up the code base while it was still readable.

glossary.kei truck: A very small utility truck; the article uses the term for the KEI-01.
glossary.rebadged: A vehicle made by one company but sold under a different brand or name.
glossary.CVT: Continuously Variable Transmission: a car system that changes how engine power reaches the wheels without fixed gear steps.
glossary.4WD: Four-wheel drive: a system that sends power to all four wheels to help a vehicle move over rough ground.
glossary.payload: The piece of code or data a request carries or delivers.
glossary.low-speed vehicle: A vehicle approved for roads with low speed limits; the article says this one is only legal on roads posted below 35 mph.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.OSS: Open-source software: software whose code is shared so others can inspect it and sometimes reuse it under a license.
glossary.true positive rate: The share of reports that turn out to describe real problems.
glossary.triage: Sorting incoming requests so the important or urgent ones get handled first.
glossary.B2B: Business-to-business: selling products or services to other companies, rather than individual people.
glossary.IoT: Internet of Things: everyday devices connected to the internet so they can share information or be controlled remotely.
glossary.static IP: An internet address that stays the same, so other systems can reliably find a device.
glossary.NAT: Network address translation: a way for a server to pass your connection along using its own internet address, so the next server doesn't see yours.
glossary.cease-and-desist letter: A formal legal demand to stop doing something.
glossary.codec: A set of rules that shrinks video for storage or sending and turns it back into a playable picture.
glossary.OIN: Open Invention Network: a group that offers patent protections to members working with Linux.
glossary.clean-room implementation: Software built independently without copying the original code.
glossary.claim chart: A document showing how parts of someone’s work supposedly relate to specific patent claims.
glossary.cloud computing: Computing that happens on remote computers, which you use over the internet.
glossary.read-only mode: A setting where you can look at things but can’t change them.
glossary.open-source: Software whose code is shared publicly so people can inspect it, change it, or build on it.
glossary.RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: a way for an AI to look up material and use it when answering.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.AST: Abstract Syntax Tree: a tree-shaped version of a program that a computer can inspect and work through.
glossary.legacy-scan: A check that looks for old code patterns an agent could update.
glossary.latchkey kid: A child who comes home from school to an empty house and lets themselves in.
glossary.surveillance capitalism: Making money by collecting information about people's behavior and using it to target or influence them.
glossary.data broker: A company that gathers information about people and sells or shares it.
glossary.isometric view: A way of drawing a place from an angle that shows rooftops and building sides at once.
glossary.pixel art: Pictures built from visible colored squares, often with a blocky look.
glossary.diffusion-art: A label for images generated or changed with AI, rather than drawn pixel by pixel by hand.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.municipal term: The official area a municipality governs, including land beyond its built-up center.
glossary.out-of-order structures: The CPU's work area for tracking instructions, so it can do ready tasks while other work waits.
glossary.CCD: Core Complex Die: a small chip inside a processor package that holds a group of CPU cores.
glossary.L3 cache: A processor's shared stash of data, meant to save trips to main memory.
glossary.branch predictor: A CPU part that guesses which way a program will go next, letting the processor get a head start.
glossary.memory latency: The time the processor spends waiting for data from memory.
glossary.VNNI: Vector Neural Network Instructions: special processor commands used for number-heavy tasks such as the AI and video work mentioned here.
glossary.NUMA: Non-Uniform Memory Access: a way of organizing processors so some can reach certain memory more quickly than others.
glossary.quantitative thinking: Using numbers to describe, compare, or work through questions about the world.
glossary.abstraction: When you don't have to deal with the messy details of how something gets done.
glossary.geometry: Math about shapes, distances, and space.
glossary.probability: A way to reason about how likely something is to happen.
glossary.analysis: A branch of math for working with very large or very small quantities.
glossary.dynamics: The part of math that looks at change.
glossary.STEM: Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics: subjects about how the world works, how to build things, and numbers.
glossary.process tree: A view showing which programs started other programs.
glossary.DLLs/images: Files containing pieces of code a program loads while it runs.
glossary.handles/file descriptors: References a program uses to keep track of things it has opened, like files or connections.
glossary.privileged helper: A companion program that can do tasks needing more permission than the main app has.
glossary.certified query: A question asked of company data that the data team has approved for everyone to reuse.
glossary.data connector: A link that lets Claude get information from another system.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service: software you access over the internet, with the provider running it for you.
glossary.carbon budget: The amount of CO2 that can still be emitted before warming reaches a stated limit.
glossary.land-use change: A change in how land is used, such as deforestation.
glossary.carbon sink: Land or ocean that absorbs CO2 from the air.
glossary.zero data retention (ZDR): Zero data retention: a promise that a service won’t keep the requests and replies sent to it.
glossary.CSV: Comma-separated values: a way to arrange data in rows, with commas separating the pieces.
glossary.API key: A secret code that lets software use an online service as an approved user.
glossary.inference: When an AI uses what it learned to answer or act, instead of being trained.
glossary.open-weight model: A model whose trained settings are shared so other people can use them.
glossary.workspace: A saved work area that keeps a project’s files or conversations together.
glossary.inference server: A computer that runs an AI model and sends its answers to other devices or apps.
glossary.unified memory: A shared pool of working memory that a computer's main processor and graphics processor can both use, instead of each having a separate pool.
glossary.Thunderbolt 5: A way to connect devices; here, it links Macs so they can work together.
glossary.private preview: An early, limited release people can try before a public launch.
glossary.vibe-coded: Made by steering an AI with informal requests instead of writing most of the code by hand.
glossary.tech debt: Extra cleanup work left behind when software choices make future changes harder.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.PR: Pull request: a proposed code change shared so others can review it.
glossary.literate programming: A way of presenting code alongside explanations so people can read why it works.
glossary.STS: Standard Term Support: a release type with a shorter support period than Long Term Support.
glossary.LTS: Long-term support: a release its makers promise to support for an extended period.
glossary.runtime async: A way for a program to handle waiting work while still doing other things.
glossary.state machine: A system that remembers its current settings, so later commands can behave differently depending on earlier ones.
glossary.lobbying: Trying to influence government decisions by making a case to officials.
glossary.mass surveillance: Watching lots of people, often by collecting information about them, rather than focusing on one person.
glossary.PATRIOT Act: A US law that expanded government surveillance powers after the 9/11 attacks.
glossary.DINO: A put-down for a Democrat someone thinks is acting more like a Republican.
glossary.ICE: Internal Combustion Engine: an engine that makes power by burning fuel inside it.
